output:
## One Assignment

Jess texted me last night: “It’s one assignment. Don’t torch your job over it.”

Then about half the group chat more or less agreed with her, which was annoying but not surprising. Jess is usually the person telling me to eat dinner before I send an email I’ll regret. We met student teaching at the same school in 2012, so she has seen nearly every version of me that thinks a well-designed unit can fix a broken system. She left teaching in 2019 and now does HR at a biotech in Cambridge. She knows schools, she knows workplaces, and she knows me. I understand why she said it.

I’m not even sure she’s wrong about the risk. I just don’t think “it’s one assignment” is quite right.

The assignment is for my juniors in US History II, two sections at Cobb Street High. Each student interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about busing and desegregation in Boston in 1974–76. They make a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. I’ve been doing it for four years. Until now, no one has complained.

Last week, a parent emailed my principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and cc’d a school committee member. She said the project “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.” Halvorsen would like me to quietly drop it. We have a meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

I’m not going to drop it. I am going to change it.

Before I get into why, I want to say that I don’t think the parent is being ridiculous. I’m not casting her as the villain in my personal academic-freedom movie. She has a point about pressure. Family history is not the same as other course material. If you ask a sixteen-year-old to interview a grandparent about busing, you might be asking them to start a conversation nobody in that house has wanted to have for fifty years. The student may learn something painful. The relative may feel ambushed. The student may then feel responsible for managing both the relative’s feelings and their own.

That’s a real burden, and I don’t get to wave it away by saying the history matters.

So from here on, no student will have to interview a family member. Students who want another route can interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recorded interviews from previous years, with permission. The alternate option won’t be a lesser assignment or something a kid has to earn by explaining their private family situation to me. It will simply be another way to do the project.

I should have built that in from the beginning. Honestly, I thought offering family *or neighborhood* interviews was enough flexibility. This complaint made me see that it wasn’t, or at least that I hadn’t made the flexibility real enough. I can admit that without concluding that the whole project should disappear.

Because the history does matter. This is the history of the city my students live in. Some of them take buses through neighborhoods whose names carry an entire political argument their textbook reduces to one paragraph. One paragraph. Then we move on, as if Boston in 1974 is just a brief, unfortunate stop between the civil rights movement and whatever comes next in the pacing guide.

Oral history makes that paragraph harder to skim.

In 2023, D. interviewed his grandmother, who drove a school bus in Southie in ’74. She had never told the family about it. Not the sanitized version, not the funny version—nothing. D. came into class afterward looking like he wasn’t sure whether he’d found something valuable or broken something. With her permission, he played forty seconds of the recording for us.

I won’t try to reproduce what she said. I’d get it wrong, and it isn’t mine. It was the sound of someone remembering that she had been afraid, and that other people had been afraid, and that fear had not made everyone behave well.

D. stopped the recording. Nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute. Teenagers can certainly be silent, especially at 8:10 in the morning, but this wasn’t that. They were actually sitting with it.

That’s the classroom moment I reach for when I try to explain the assignment, which is a little dangerous, because it makes the project sound cleaner and more moving than it always is. Sometimes the audio is terrible. Sometimes an uncle talks for nine minutes about the price of gas. Sometimes a student does the reflection at lunch and writes, “I learned that busing was controversial,” and I have to pretend not to die inside.

And sometimes it hurts.

Last year, a girl in one of my sections found out that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She was upset—not in a productive, cinematic, “now I understand the complexity of history” way. Just upset. We talked after class twice. I told her she could change the project. I told her she didn’t have to use the interview, told me she didn’t have to defend him, and told her she didn’t have to turn him into a monster for a grade either.

She stayed with it. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. Not because she reached some conclusion I agreed with, and not because she condemned her uncle in the properly educational language. It was good because she refused to make the story simpler than it was. She loved him. She hated what he had done. She understood some of what had surrounded him without using any of it as an excuse. She was still angry at him when she wrote it.

I don’t know whether every student should have to do that. Actually, no—I do know. They shouldn’t.

The teacher in me believes the kids who flinch at this material are often the ones who have the most to gain from being given a careful way into it. But that belief can turn arrogant very quickly. Discomfort is not automatically educational. A kid’s distress is not evidence that my lesson is working. I don’t get to force a family reckoning because I think it would build character or deepen someone’s understanding of American history. That’s the line for me. I can open the door. I can make sure there are other doors. I cannot push a kid through and call it rigor.

What I don’t want to do is quietly take the project away from every student because one part of it wasn’t designed carefully enough.

There’s something else, too, and I’m trying to be honest about it. It would be easier to drop the assignment. Not in every way—I’d be furious with myself for a while—but practically, yes. The email stops mattering. The meeting gets shorter. I keep my head down and teach the paragraph in the textbook.

I’m tenured, and have been since 2021, so this is not quite the story of somebody gambling her entire livelihood on a two-page reflection. But tenure doesn’t mean Halvorsen has no power over my working life. My principal still controls my schedule and who gets AP. I know what it can cost to become the teacher who is “difficult,” especially when a school committee member has already been cc’d. Jess knows that too. That’s part of why her text got under my skin: it wasn’t coming from someone who thinks principals are just friendly instructional leaders who want what’s best for everyone.

I’m scared, a little. I don’t feel brave about this. I keep composing Thursday’s meeting in my head while I’m driving and then losing my whole train of thought because someone merges without looking. I have imagined being calm and persuasive, and I have imagined hearing my own voice get high and defensive about ninety seconds in. Both seem entirely possible.

I’m also not interested in turning this into a test of whether I care enough about justice. People who teach for a long time learn to be suspicious of that particular story, or at least I hope they do. You can burn yourself out, alienate everyone around you, and still leave behind a mediocre unit. Wanting to keep my job does not make me a coward. Wanting to keep the assignment does not automatically make me right.

But I think I am right about this much: Boston students should have a chance to hear Boston history from people who were there. Not only the people whose names made it into official accounts. A grandmother who drove a bus. A neighbor who stood on a corner. A parent who transferred schools. Someone who was nineteen and furious and now isn’t sure what to make of the person they were. Someone whose memory contradicts another memory across town.

The point isn’t to make kids judge their grandparents. It’s to let them discover that their grandparents were there. Those are very different projects.

Jess, I’m not asking you to agree with me, though obviously I’d enjoy it if you did. I’m asking you to understand that I’m not trying to torch anything. I’m trying to fix the part that deserves fixing and defend the part I think is worth keeping. If I give up the whole thing now, the easiest lesson for everyone to take is that this history is fine as long as it stays abstract and distant, and becomes a problem when somebody’s actual grandmother starts talking.

I don’t want to teach that lesson.

So Thursday at 3:15, I’ll go in with the alternate options, the complaint, four years of student work, and probably too many notes. I’ll listen. I’ll try not to talk like I’m defending a dissertation. I’ll see what happens.

And I’ll text you afterward. Probably something very articulate like, “Well, that was a meeting.” You can tell me then whether I handled it like a professional or like the person you had to stop from arguing with a cooperating teacher in 2012.

I’ll be annoyed, and then I’ll probably listen.
